summary: Describes loop-free alternates, a way to give routers local protection for unicast traffic in IP and MPLS/LDP networks when a link, node, or shared risk link group fails. A router precomputes a backup next hop that will not send traffic back, so it can switch immediately and cut packet loss while the network reconverges.

plainLanguage.summary: Loop-free alternates let a router switch to a precomputed backup path when its primary path fails. The backup can reduce packet loss while routers calculate new routes, but coverage depends on the network layout.

questions: how routers recover quickly from link failure
how do routers avoid micro-loops after a link failure
subtitle: How routers precompute loop-free backup next hops for traffic affected by a local failure.

tldr.problem: After a link or router fails, routers need time to update their routes. During that time, packets for affected destinations may be discarded.
tldr.mechanism: A router calculates loop-free alternate next hops before a failure. When its primary next hop fails, it can send traffic through a suitable alternate while the routing system converges.
tldr.outcome: The approach needs no support from other routers, but which destinations it can protect depends on the network topology. RFC 5286 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 8518.

today: RFC 5286 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 8518.

sections.title: Why Routers Need Fast Reroute
sections.content:
When a link or router fails, a link-state routing system must learn about the change, recalculate routes and install new next hops. Traffic for affected destinations may be discarded during that process. The RFC notes that convergence generally takes hundreds of milliseconds, while some applications are sensitive to losses lasting tens of milliseconds.

IP Fast Reroute aims to reduce this loss by calculating a backup next hop before a failure. The router switches to that alternate when it detects that its primary next hop has failed, then returns to new primary routes after the network converges. This specification assumes OSPF or IS-IS routing and paths within the same area.
sections.plainLanguage: A router normally has to recalculate routes after a failure, and packets may be lost while it does so. A precomputed alternate lets it switch paths sooner.

sections.title: What Failures an Alternate Can Protect Against
sections.content:
An alternate may protect against a link failure, a node failure, or a failure involving links in a shared risk link group. Protection depends on the failure the alternate was chosen to handle. If a larger or simultaneous failure occurs, traffic may briefly loop until a complete shortest-path calculation finishes.

A node-protecting alternate avoids the primary neighbor as well as the calculating router. A downstream path is stricter: the next router must already be closer to the destination. This prevents micro-loops involving the calculating router, but can leave fewer destinations protected. The RFC also describes local shared-risk groups whose links all connect to the same router.
sections.plainLanguage: A backup may protect against a failed link, a failed router or a group of related links. A backup designed for one failure may not be safe when a larger failure happens.

sections.title: Testing Whether a Neighbor Is Loop-Free
sections.content:
Let S be the router choosing an alternate, N a neighbor and D the destination. N is a loop-free alternate when its shortest path to D is shorter than the route from N through S to D: Distance_opt(N,D) < Distance_opt(N,S) + Distance_opt(S,D). This ensures that N's shortest path to the destination does not return through S.

To protect against failure of primary neighbor E, N must also satisfy Distance_opt(N,D) < Distance_opt(N,E) + Distance_opt(E,D). On broadcast or non-broadcast multi-access links, the router must consider the link's pseudo-node and ensure both the alternate route and the path to the alternate avoid the failed link when link protection is required.

Routers obtain needed distances from their normal shortest-path calculation and additional calculations rooted at neighbors. They must not choose next hops that use links costed out for maintenance or overloaded IS-IS routers.
sections.plainLanguage: A neighbor is a safe alternate only when its shortest route to the destination does not lead back through the router choosing it. Node protection adds a check that the alternate route also avoids the failed neighbor.

sections.title: Selecting an Alternate
sections.content:
A router should try to select at least one loop-free alternate for each primary next hop. It should prefer an alternate that protects against both link and node failure. If none is available, it may choose a link-protecting alternate. When several primary next hops exist, another primary or a node-protecting alternate is preferred when suitable.

The router may consider shared-risk link groups when selecting an alternate. The RFC provides one selection procedure for information, but implementations may use another algorithm that follows the stated rules. A simpler calculation can choose one link-protecting alternate per next hop, but may protect fewer prefixes.
sections.plainLanguage: The router prefers backups that survive more types of failure. It may choose another safe option when the strongest protection is unavailable, and the RFC allows different calculation algorithms.

sections.title: Switching to and Leaving the Alternate
sections.content:
When a router detects that a primary next hop has failed, it should remove that next hop and install its calculated alternate if needed. It may use the alternate only for traffic routed on shortest paths; multicast is outside this specification.

A router must limit how long it uses an alternate. It should keep using it until the new routes are safe, a configured hold-down expires or an unrelated topology change is reported. Switching too early can send traffic to a neighbor that has not updated its own route yet, creating a temporary loop.

For LDP traffic to use the alternate, labels for that path must already be available before the failure. The RFC describes distributing labels to all neighbors and retaining labels that do not currently correspond to primary next hops.
sections.plainLanguage: When the primary next hop fails, the router installs the alternate and uses it while the network updates its routes. It stops using the alternate after a defined condition, so it does not switch back before other routers are ready.

sections.title: Routing Scope and Special Cases
sections.content:
The specification applies to intra-domain routing with OSPF or IS-IS. It does not define fast reroute for inter-domain BGP, and multicast is out of scope. BGP routes can inherit an alternate for their IGP next hop without changing the BGP decision process.

Multi-homed prefixes may need a calculation that considers all routers announcing the prefix. OSPF's multi-area routes also create cases where a path leaves an area and returns, so the RFC lists conditions where alternates should not be used. Multi-topology OSPF and IS-IS are outside the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC covers specific unicast routes inside a routing domain using OSPF or IS-IS. It excludes multicast and inter-domain BGP rerouting and sets extra limits for some multi-area OSPF routes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanism does not change routing protocol messages, so the RFC says it introduces no new threats involving message modification or replay. Some traffic may temporarily pass through a next-hop router that would not be selected under the unchanged topology, but the RFC does not consider that a new security threat.

LDP may distribute labels to more neighbors, but the labels still go only to neighbors with trusted LDP sessions. The RFC considers this and liberal label retention to have no significant security impact.
sections.plainLanguage: The mechanism does not alter routing messages. For LDP, it shares labels more widely among trusted neighbors, which the RFC says has no significant security impact.

data.title: Conditions for neighbor N, router S, destination D and failed neighbor E
data.code:
Loop-free:  Distance_opt(N,D) < Distance_opt(N,S) + Distance_opt(S,D)
Node-protecting: Distance_opt(N,D) < Distance_opt(N,E) + Distance_opt(E,D)
